books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence

stimulus.text: This lithograph, entered in 1840, shows the Battle of New Orleans on January 8, 1815. American troops fire from behind earthworks along the Mississippi River while British soldiers advance in formation across an open field. The title printed below the image reads “BATTLE OF NEW-ORLEANS. January 8th 1815.”
stimulus.source_note: Battle of New Orleans, lithograph by P. S. Duval after Laclotte, drawn on stone by A. Hoffy, entered 1840; public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The fact that this lithograph was published in 1840, a generation after the battle, best suggests that

options.text: Americans were eager to celebrate the victory as a national triumph
the battle was still being fought in 1840
options.misconception: The battle lasted one day, January 8, 1815.

options.text: the lithograph was made as a British report on the defeat
options.misconception: It was published in Philadelphia for an American audience.

options.text: Jackson had ordered the lithograph as a campaign poster
options.misconception: Jackson ran for president in 1828, not 1840, and no evidence ties him to the print.

rationales.A: A detailed battle print published twenty-five years later, for buyers in American cities, shows a public still hungry for images of the victory. The battle became the war's most celebrated moment.
rationales.B: The title dates the battle January 8, 1815. Nothing was still being fought twenty-five years later.
rationales.C: The lithograph was published in Philadelphia by an American firm, for Americans proud of the victory, not as a British report.
rationales.D: Jackson's presidential campaigns came in 1824 and 1828. In 1840 he was a former president, not a candidate ordering posters.
rationales.general: 1. Read the dates. The battle was January 8, 1815, and the print came out in 1840. 2. Ask who buys a battle print twenty-five years later. People who still want to celebrate a victory do. 3. Put it together. A market for heroic prints a generation on shows a public that kept celebrating. Background: The victory fed postwar nationalism, and Jackson's fame from it carried him to the presidency in 1828. Remember: when a victory is still pictured a generation later, ask what the audience wanted to remember.
